questions.stem: A 34 year old man has a 3 day history of fever, headache and vomiting. He returned from visiting relatives in Lagos, Nigeria 11 days ago and took no prophylaxis. His temperature is 39.1°C and pulse rate 112 bpm. A thin blood film shows many red cells containing small ring-shaped inclusions, some with two rings in one cell.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Ring-shaped inclusions, often several in one red cell, in a traveller from sub-Saharan Africa are P. falciparum, the most common and most dangerous species.

steps.x: West Africa + no prophylaxis + **ring forms** on thin film = **P. falciparum**.

elim: Babesia is tick-borne in North America and Europe, not acquired in Nigeria.
P. malariae is uncommon and shows band forms, not multiple rings per cell.
P. ovale gives oval enlarged red cells with fewer parasites.
P. vivax enlarges red cells and is rare in West Africa.

steps.x: **B. Plasmodium falciparum.** Ring-shaped inclusions on smear = P. falciparum.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman has a 2 day history of fever, rigors and muscle aches. She returned from a 3 week safari in Tanzania 8 days ago and stopped her prophylaxis early. Her temperature is 38.9°C and pulse rate 108 bpm. A rapid antigen test is positive for P. falciparum. A thin blood film is examined.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the thin film?
o: Enlarged red cells with Schüffner's dots
questions.e: P. falciparum shows ring-shaped inclusions within normal-sized red cells on thin film; Schüffner's dots belong to vivax and ovale.

steps.x: Antigen test says **falciparum**; the classic thin film finding is **ring forms**.

elim: Gametocytes appear later; early infection shows ring forms.
Schüffner's dots are seen with P. vivax and P. ovale.
These are leishmaniasis in macrophages, not red cells.
Extracellular trypanosomes are sleeping sickness.

steps.x: **D. Ring-shaped inclusions in red cells.** Thin film identifies the species: falciparum = ring-shaped inclusions.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man has P. falciparum malaria after a business trip to Ghana. He is alert. His temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 104/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. He has passed little urine today. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely classification of his illness?
questions.e: Renal failure and metabolic acidosis are features of severe malaria, which P. falciparum most commonly causes, even though he is alert.

steps.x: Rapid breathing with **low bicarbonate** = **acidosis**. Little urine + rising creatinine = **AKI**. Either makes falciparum **severe**.

elim: Blackwater fever is haemoglobinuria; it does not account for his acidosis and AKI.
He is alert with no neurological signs.
Vivax relapse does not happen with falciparum, which has no hypnozoites.
Renal failure and acidosis make it severe, whatever his parasitaemia.

steps.x: **D. Severe falciparum malaria.** Severe malaria: hypoglycaemia <2.2, reduced consciousness, severe anaemia, acidosis, renal failure, neurology.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman has 4 days of fever, headache and malaise. She returned from Kenya 10 days ago and took no prophylaxis. Her fever has no regular pattern. Her temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. Her spleen is not palpable. Her platelet count is 88 × 10⁹/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Early falciparum malaria often has an irregular fever and no splenomegaly; sub-Saharan Africa within 2 weeks of return makes falciparum most likely.

steps.x: Sub-Saharan Africa + short incubation + **irregular fever** + **no spleen yet** = early falciparum.

elim: P. malariae is uncommon and has a long, regular cycle.
P. ovale is less common in East Africa and gives regular 48 hour fevers.
Vivax is rare in East Africa and gives regular fevers.
Typhoid has a slower stepwise fever with relative bradycardia, and less marked thrombocytopenia.

steps.x: **A. Plasmodium falciparum.** No splenomegaly does not exclude falciparum: early infection often has none.

questions.stem: A 31 year old man sees his GP with 3 days of fever, headache and aching muscles. He thinks he has flu. He is a nurse who returned from 6 weeks volunteering in Sierra Leone 2 weeks ago. His temperature is 38.6°C and pulse rate 102 bpm. His chest is clear and he has no rash.
questions.q: Which feature of the history is the most important clue to the diagnosis?
questions.e: Fever in a traveller returning from an endemic area, especially sub-Saharan Africa, is malaria until proven otherwise; the travel history is the single most important clue.

clues: returned from 6 weeks volunteering in Sierra Leone
steps.x: Fever + **returned from sub-Saharan Africa** = malaria until three films are negative.

elim: Myalgia is non-specific and seen in any viral illness.
Headache is non-specific and does not point to a cause.
His job matters less than where he has been.
The duration fits many infections.

steps.x: **D. Recent travel to sub-Saharan Africa.** Travel history is the single most important clue in malaria.

questions.stem: A 23 year old woman develops fever and rigors 12 days after returning from a gap-year trip to Malawi. She remembers many insect bites at dusk and in the night. She had no blood transfusion or injections abroad. A thick blood film shows Plasmodium parasites.
questions.q: Which is the most likely way she acquired the infection?
o: Bite of a female Anopheles mosquito
questions.e: Plasmodium sporozoites are injected by the female Anopheles mosquito, which bites at dusk and at night.

clues: insect bites at dusk and in the night
steps.x: **Plasmodium** + **night-time bites** = female **Anopheles**.

elim: Aedes bites by day and transmits dengue, Zika and chikungunya.
Sandflies transmit leishmaniasis.
Tsetse flies transmit African trypanosomiasis.
Malaria is not transmitted by the faecal-oral route.

steps.x: **C. Bite of a female Anopheles mosquito.** Malaria: Plasmodium transmitted by the female Anopheles mosquito.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man has 5 days of fever and rigors after a trip to Cameroon. He is jaundiced and has passed only 200 mL of urine in 24 hours. His temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 124 bpm and BP 96/58 mmHg. He did not swim in rivers. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Ring forms with high parasitaemia, jaundice and acute kidney injury after travel to Central Africa are severe falciparum malaria, a leading cause of malarial renal failure.

steps.x: Jaundice + **AKI** have several tropical causes, but **ring forms** on the film settle it: severe falciparum.

elim: HUS follows bloody diarrhoea and would not show parasites.
Leptospirosis can cause jaundice and AKI but he did not swim and films show parasites.
Typhoid rarely causes jaundice with AKI and does not show ring forms.
Yellow fever causes jaundice and AKI but no parasites on the film.

steps.x: **C. Severe P. falciparum malaria.** Falciparum is the most common cause of severe malaria, including AKI and cerebral malaria.

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman has 4 days of vomiting, diarrhoea and fever after returning from Ghana 10 days ago. She has had several episodes of shaking chills followed by drenching sweats. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. Her liver and spleen are both palpable. Her stool contains no blood.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Gastrointestinal symptoms are common in malaria; rigors with sweats and hepatosplenomegaly after travel to West Africa make malaria the diagnosis, not gastroenteritis.

clues: shaking chills followed by drenching sweats
liver and spleen are both palpable
steps.x: Diarrhoea can mislead; **rigors + sweats** and **hepatosplenomegaly** after Ghana = malaria.

elim: Amoebic dysentery gives bloody diarrhoea and does not cause rigors with hepatosplenomegaly.
Dengue has a short incubation, rash and retro-orbital pain, without rigors and hepatosplenomegaly.
Traveller's diarrhoea does not cause rigors or hepatosplenomegaly.
Influenza does not cause hepatosplenomegaly and is not linked to travel.

steps.x: **E. Malaria.** Malaria often presents with vomiting and diarrhoea; always ask about travel.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man has P. falciparum malaria after a trip to Uganda. He is alert and orientated. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 122/74 mmHg. His glucose is 5.2 mmol/L and creatinine is normal. Investigations:
questions.q: Which result best indicates severe malaria?
questions.e: Severe anaemia is a feature of severe malaria; mild thrombocytopenia is common in any malaria and parasitaemia below 2% fits uncomplicated disease.

steps.x: He is alert with normal glucose and kidneys, so look for **another severe feature**: **severe anaemia**.

elim: Below 2% parasitaemia is consistent with uncomplicated malaria.
Thrombocytopenia is common in malaria and does not on its own define severity.
Mild hyperbilirubinaemia from haemolysis is common and not a severe feature.
A fever below 39°C is not a severe feature.

steps.x: **C. Haemoglobin 61 g/L.** Severe features include severe anaemia, hypoglycaemia <2.2, acidosis, AKI, reduced consciousness.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman is brought in drowsy 2 weeks after returning from Mozambique. She has had fevers for 5 days. Her GCS is 9 with no neck stiffness or rash. Her temperature is 39.8°C, pulse rate 128 bpm and BP 100/62 mmHg. Glucose is 5.8 mmol/L. CT head is normal and CSF shows normal cells, protein and glucose.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Reduced consciousness with fever after travel to sub-Saharan Africa, normal glucose, CT and CSF is cerebral malaria, the key complication of falciparum.

clues: CSF shows normal cells, protein and glucose
steps.x: Coma + fever + Africa with **normal glucose and normal CSF** = cerebral malaria.

elim: The CSF has normal cells, protein and glucose, and there is no neck stiffness.
HSV encephalitis usually raises the CSF lymphocyte count.
Her glucose is 5.8 mmol/L.
CT is normal and there was no thunderclap headache.

steps.x: **B. Cerebral malaria.** Any reduced consciousness or neurology in falciparum = severe (cerebral) malaria.

questions.stem: A 39 year old man has 3 days of fever, headache and rigors after returning from Burkina Faso. His temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 106 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg. His spleen tip is palpable. Thick and thin films are sent, together with a full blood count.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on his full blood count?
questions.e: Thrombocytopenia (and anaemia) are the usual FBC findings in malaria; eosinophilia points to a worm infection instead.

steps.x: Febrile traveller from West Africa with rigors and a spleen = malaria, whose classic FBC is **low platelets**.

elim: Eosinophilia suggests helminths such as schistosomiasis, not malaria.
Malaria rarely raises the neutrophil count.
Malaria causes anaemia, not polycythaemia.
Platelets fall, rather than rise, in malaria.

steps.x: **D. Thrombocytopenia.** FBC in malaria: anaemia and thrombocytopenia.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman has P. falciparum malaria after a holiday in The Gambia. She is alert, eating and drinking, and has not vomited. Her temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely classification of her malaria?
questions.e: Falciparum with parasitaemia below 2% and no severe features (normal glucose, Hb, renal function and consciousness) is uncomplicated and can be treated orally.

steps.x: Check the severe features one by one: **none present** and parasitaemia **<2%** = uncomplicated.

elim: She is alert with no neurological features.
Her parasitaemia is below 2%.
The film confirms P. falciparum.
She has none of the severe features: glucose, Hb, kidneys and consciousness are fine.

steps.x: **E. Uncomplicated falciparum malaria.** Uncomplicated falciparum: <2% parasitaemia and no severe features.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man is admitted with P. falciparum malaria after a trip to Nigeria. His parasitaemia is 6% and he has started IV artesunate. He is currently alert. His temperature is 39.5°C, pulse rate 122 bpm and BP 108/66 mmHg. The nurse asks which complication to watch for most closely.
questions.q: Which complication is he at greatest risk of?
questions.e: High-parasitaemia falciparum malaria carries a high risk of cerebral malaria, the key complication to watch for, along with AKI.

steps.x: Falciparum + high parasitaemia + high fever = biggest risk is **cerebral malaria**.

elim: Endocarditis is not a complication of malaria.
Liver abscess is amoebic or bacterial, not malarial.
PE is not a recognised specific risk of falciparum.
Rupture is rare and more linked to vivax with a large spleen.

steps.x: **A. Cerebral malaria.** Watch every falciparum patient for cerebral malaria: check GCS and glucose.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man has fevers every other day for a week. He was treated for malaria with chloroquine alone after returning from India 9 months ago and has not travelled since. His temperature is 38.6°C and his spleen is palpable. A thin film shows enlarged red cells with Schüffner's dots.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Relapse months after chloroquine alone, without new travel, is due to dormant liver hypnozoites; P. vivax is the species from India that does this.

steps.x: Illness **months later with no new travel** = relapse from **hypnozoites**. From India = **vivax**.

elim: Falciparum does not form hypnozoites and so does not relapse months later.
P. knowlesi is from South-East Asia, has a 24 hour cycle and does not relapse.
P. malariae can persist but does not form liver hypnozoites or Schüffner's dots.
Ovale also relapses but is mainly from West Africa, not India.

steps.x: **E. Plasmodium vivax.** P. vivax relapses from dormant hypnozoites unless primaquine is given.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man has fever and rigors 3 weeks after returning from Papua New Guinea. A thick blood film shows malaria parasites. The laboratory now needs to know which Plasmodium species is responsible before treatment is chosen.
questions.q: Which investigation will best identify the species?
questions.e: Thick films detect parasites and assess burden; thin films show red cell morphology and identify the species.

clues: thick blood film shows malaria parasites
steps.x: Thick = **how many** (burden). Thin = **which one** (species).

elim: Plasmodium does not grow in blood culture.
Serology shows past exposure, not current species.
Thick films assess parasite burden, not species.
Malaria is a blood parasite; stool shows nothing.

steps.x: **E. Thin blood film.** Thick film: parasite burden. Thin film: species.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman with P. falciparum malaria confirmed on thin film after a trip to Benin is alert and well perfused. The team needs to decide whether she can have oral treatment and wants to quantify her parasite burden.
questions.q: Which investigation best assesses her parasite burden?
questions.e: The thick film assesses parasite burden; below 2% parasitaemia, with no severe features, is uncomplicated and suits oral therapy.

steps.x: Species is already known from the thin film; **burden** comes from the **thick film**.

elim: Plasmodium cannot be cultured in routine blood cultures.
LDH rises with haemolysis but does not count parasites.
Antigen tests are qualitative and do not measure burden.
Bilirubin reflects haemolysis, not parasite numbers.

steps.x: **E. Thick blood film.** Parasitaemia below 2% = uncomplicated (if no severe features).

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has had fevers for 4 days since returning from Zambia 10 days ago. His temperature is 38.9°C and pulse rate 104 bpm. A thick and thin blood film taken this morning is negative. He took no prophylaxis. The registrar wants to know when malaria can be safely ruled out.
questions.q: Which is the minimum needed before malaria is excluded?
o: Three negative film sets over 24 to 48 hours
Two negative film sets a week apart
questions.e: If films are negative but suspicion remains, repeat them up to 3 times over 24 to 48 hours before ruling malaria out.

steps.x: One negative film in a high-risk traveller is not enough: **3 sets over 24 to 48 h**.

elim: One negative film does not exclude malaria when suspicion remains.
A week is far too long to wait in possible falciparum.
Serology is not used to exclude acute malaria.
Blood cultures do not detect Plasmodium.

steps.x: **D. Three negative film sets over 24 to 48 hours.** Malaria is only excluded after 3 negative films over 24 to 48 hours.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman has fever and rigors 9 days after returning from Côte d'Ivoire. Her temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg. She is alert. Thick and thin blood films have been sent urgently.
questions.q: Which set of tests should also be sent at the same time?
questions.e: Alongside blood films, send FBC (anaemia, thrombocytopenia), U&Es (renal failure) and glucose (hypoglycaemia), which help grade severity.

clues: Thick and thin blood films have been sent
steps.x: Films diagnose; **FBC, U&Es and glucose** look for anaemia, AKI and hypoglycaemia, the severe features.

elim: She has no respiratory symptoms.
She is alert with no meningism.
Serology has no role in acute diagnosis.
She has no gastrointestinal symptoms.

steps.x: **B. FBC, U&Es and glucose.** First-line bloods with films: FBC, U&Es, glucose.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man has 2 days of fever and headache after returning from Ghana 2 weeks ago. His temperature is 38.7°C and pulse rate 100 bpm. A rapid diagnostic antigen test done in the Emergency Department is negative. He did not take prophylaxis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: Repeat rapid antigen test in 1 week
questions.e: Thick and thin blood film microscopy is the gold standard for malaria; a negative rapid test does not exclude it in a febrile traveller from West Africa.

steps.x: A negative rapid test does not exclude malaria. The **gold standard** is **microscopy of thick and thin films**.

elim: Blood cultures look for bacteraemia, not Plasmodium.
Serology shows past exposure and cannot diagnose acute malaria.
Waiting a week risks progression to severe falciparum.
There is no urine test for malaria.

steps.x: **D. Thick and thin blood films.** Gold standard for malaria: thick and thin blood films.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman has uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria acquired in an area with known chloroquine resistance. She is alert, eating and drinking and has parasitaemia of 0.5%. She is not pregnant. The ward does not stock artemisinin combinations today.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate oral treatment?
questions.e: Chloroquine-resistant uncomplicated P. falciparum can be treated orally with atovaquone-proguanil.

steps.x: Uncomplicated (oral) + **chloroquine-resistant** falciparum = **atovaquone-proguanil**.

elim: The parasite is chloroquine-resistant.
Doxycycline is used for prophylaxis or as an add-on, not alone for treatment.
IV therapy is for severe malaria; she is uncomplicated.
Primaquine treats hypnozoites of vivax and ovale, not falciparum blood stages.

steps.x: **A. Atovaquone-proguanil.** Chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum: atovaquone-proguanil.

questions.stem: A 41 year old man has fevers every 48 hours for 6 days after returning from Nigeria 3 months ago. A thin film shows enlarged oval red cells with Schüffner's dots, reported as P. ovale, with low parasitaemia. He is alert and eating. The species is not known to be resistant.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.e: Non-resistant P. ovale and P. vivax are treated with oral chloroquine, followed by primaquine to clear hypnozoites.

steps.x: **Ovale**, uncomplicated, **non-resistant** = **chloroquine** first, primaquine after.

elim: Doxycycline is for falciparum prophylaxis, not treatment of ovale.
Exchange transfusion is a second-line option in severe falciparum.
He has uncomplicated non-falciparum malaria.
Primaquine clears liver hypnozoites but does not treat the blood stage.

steps.x: **D. Oral chloroquine.** Non-resistant vivax/ovale: chloroquine, then primaquine.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman is going backpacking in rural Tanzania for 6 weeks. She asks her GP for malaria prophylaxis. She is not pregnant, has no medical problems and is happy to take a daily tablet, continuing it for 4 weeks after return. She is willing to use sunscreen.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate prophylaxis?
questions.e: Doxycycline is used for prophylaxis against blood-stage P. falciparum; it is taken daily and continued for 4 weeks after return, with photosensitivity advice.

clues: daily tablet, continuing it for 4 weeks after return
steps.x: Daily tablet, **4 weeks after return**, **sunscreen** (photosensitivity) = **doxycycline**.

elim: Falciparum in East Africa is widely chloroquine-resistant.
Bite avoidance is essential but not enough on its own for rural East Africa.
Primaquine is for hypnozoite eradication in vivax/ovale, not standard falciparum prophylaxis.
Quinine is a treatment drug, not used for prophylaxis.

steps.x: **B. Doxycycline.** Doxycycline: prophylaxis against blood-stage P. falciparum.

questions.stem: A 38 year old man is in intensive care with severe P. falciparum malaria. He has been on IV artesunate for 24 hours. His GCS has fallen from 13 to 9 and his parasitaemia has risen from 18% to 26%. His creatinine is rising and he has a metabolic acidosis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional treatment?
questions.e: Exchange transfusion is a second-line option in selected severe falciparum cases, such as very high or rising parasitaemia despite IV artesunate.

steps.x: Worsening on **first-line IV artesunate** with very high parasitaemia = second-line **exchange transfusion**.

elim: Oral chloroquine is for non-resistant vivax/ovale and cannot be taken in coma.
Antibiotics do not treat the parasite.
Doxycycline alone is too slow for severe falciparum.
Primaquine targets liver hypnozoites, which falciparum does not form.

steps.x: **B. Exchange transfusion.** Severe falciparum: IV artesunate first; exchange transfusion second-line in selected cases.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman has P. falciparum malaria after visiting family in Sierra Leone. She has vomited six times today and cannot keep tablets down. She is alert. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 108/68 mmHg. Thick film parasitaemia is 3%. Glucose is 4.8 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Falciparum with parasitaemia over 2% and inability to take oral treatment needs prompt parenteral therapy: IV artesunate is first line.

clues: vomited six times today and cannot keep tablets down
steps.x: Parasitaemia **above 2%** and **cannot take tablets** = treat as severe: parenteral **IV artesunate**.

elim: She cannot keep tablets down and parasitaemia is above 2%.
Oral treatment fails if she vomits it back.
Chloroquine is for non-resistant vivax/ovale, not falciparum from West Africa.
Exchange transfusion is second-line in selected severe cases, not first line.

steps.x: **C. IV artesunate.** Severe or vomiting falciparum: IV artesunate, admit, ICU-level care if needed.

questions.stem: A 32 year old man has uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria after a trip to Kenya, with parasitaemia of 0.6% and no severe features. He is alert and eating. It is 11 pm and he asks to go home and return to clinic next week. His temperature is 38.4°C and BP 124/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Admit and start artemisinin-based combination therapy
Give IV artesunate in intensive care
Repeat blood film in 48 hours before treating
questions.e: Malaria must be treated urgently; uncomplicated P. falciparum is treated with ACT, starting now rather than waiting for clinic.

clues: asks to go home and return to clinic next week
steps.x: Falciparum can turn severe within hours, so **treat urgently**. Uncomplicated = oral **ACT**.

elim: Chloroquine is not used for falciparum, and he should not go home untreated overnight.
IV artesunate is for severe malaria; he is uncomplicated.
Primaquine does not treat falciparum blood stages.
Falciparum must be treated urgently, not watched.

steps.x: **A. Admit and start artemisinin-based combination therapy.** Uncomplicated falciparum: ACT, started promptly.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman has finished a 3 day course of chloroquine for P. vivax malaria acquired in Afghanistan. Her fever has settled and her film is now clear. Primaquine is planned to prevent relapse. She is not pregnant and has no other medical problems.
questions.q: Which investigation must be done before primaquine is started?
questions.e: Primaquine eradicates dormant liver hypnozoites in vivax/ovale but causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency, so G6PD activity is checked first.

clues: Primaquine is planned to prevent relapse
steps.x: **Primaquine** clears hypnozoites after the acute course, but can cause **haemolysis** in G6PD deficiency.

elim: Autoimmune screening does not affect primaquine safety.
Calcium and bone results do not affect primaquine use.
Iron status does not change primaquine safety.
Thyroid function does not affect primaquine use.

steps.x: **C. G6PD enzyme activity.** Before primaquine: check G6PD.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man is bitten by mosquitoes on his first night in rural Uganda. He feels well for the next 10 days and then develops fever and rigors. A blood film shows P. falciparum. He asks why he had no symptoms for so long after the bite.
questions.q: Where were the parasites most likely developing during the symptom-free period?
o: In liver cells, maturing into merozoites
In red cells, as ring forms
In the skin, as dormant hypnozoites
questions.e: Injected sporozoites travel to the liver and mature into merozoites (liver schizogony) without symptoms; symptoms begin when merozoites invade red cells.

clues: feels well for the next 10 days
steps.x: Sporozoites go **to the liver first**: liver schizogony is silent, and symptoms start when **merozoites** reach red cells.

elim: Red cell infection causes symptoms; it follows the liver stage.
Sporozoites left the mosquito when he was bitten.
Gametocytes form in blood later and are not the incubation stage.
Hypnozoites are a liver stage of vivax and ovale only.

steps.x: **A. In liver cells, maturing into merozoites.** Life cycle: sporozoites, liver schizogony, merozoites, red cell invasion.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman has had fever every 48 hours for a week, after returning from India. Each episode starts with shaking chills, then a high fever, then drenching sweats, and she feels well between them. A thin film shows P. vivax.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her periodic fevers?
o: Immune complex deposition in the kidneys
Periodic release of sporozoites from the liver
Synchronised rupture of infected red cells
questions.e: Merozoites invade red cells and multiply in synchronised cycles; the cyclical haemolysis as cells rupture releases parasites and toxins, causing the periodic fevers.

steps.x: Fevers in **regular cycles** = parasites bursting out of red cells **together** each cycle.

elim: No bacterial infection follows a regular 48 hour cycle.
Immune complexes cause glomerular disease, not periodic fever.
Sporozoites enter the liver only once, after the bite.
Hypnozoites reactivate months later, not every 2 days.

steps.x: **E. Synchronised rupture of infected red cells.** Cyclical haemolysis of red cells causes the classic periodic fevers.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man has P. falciparum malaria after a trip to Senegal. He has yellow sclerae and a palpable liver and spleen. His urine is dark and there is no history of liver disease or alcohol excess. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his jaundice?
questions.e: Red cell rupture releases haemoglobin breakdown products, causing unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with anaemia and high LDH, and contributes to hepatosplenomegaly.

steps.x: **Unconjugated** bilirubin + low Hb + **high LDH** + near-normal ALT = **haemolysis**.

elim: Obstruction raises ALP and conjugated bilirubin.
He has not started treatment, and his ALT is near normal.
Gilbert's does not cause anaemia, raised LDH or splenomegaly.
Hepatitis A raises ALT into the hundreds or thousands.

steps.x: **D. Haemolysis of infected red cells.** Malarial jaundice comes from haemolysis of infected red cells.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man is being treated for severe P. falciparum malaria with IV quinine because artesunate was not available. Six hours after starting the infusion he becomes sweaty, tremulous and confused. His capillary glucose is 1.8 mmol/L. His temperature is 38.6°C and BP 118/70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely drug-related mechanism of his hypoglycaemia?
questions.e: Quinine stimulates pancreatic insulin release; together with parasite glucose consumption and impaired hepatic gluconeogenesis, this causes hypoglycaemia in severe malaria.

clues: Six hours after starting the infusion
steps.x: The question asks for the **drug** mechanism: quinine causes **insulin release**.

elim: Adrenal haemorrhage causes shock and is not drug-related here.
An insulinoma is a pre-existing tumour, unrelated to treatment.
Quinine does not suppress cortisol.
Quinine does not cause renal glucose loss.

steps.x: **E. Quinine-stimulated insulin release.** Malaria hypoglycaemia: parasite glucose use, impaired gluconeogenesis, quinine-induced insulin release.

questions.stem: Two travellers return from Ghana with malaria. One has P. ovale with mild fever and is treated as an outpatient. The other has P. falciparum and within 48 hours is confused with rising creatinine. A student asks why falciparum causes organ failure when the other species rarely do.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Falciparum is spread by a different mosquito
Falciparum stimulates a stronger antibody response
Infected red cells adhere to vascular endothelium
questions.e: Cytoadherence of falciparum-infected red cells to endothelium causes sequestration in the brain, kidney and other microvasculature, explaining cerebral malaria, renal failure and high mortality.

steps.x: Organ failure in brain and kidney = **microvascular block** from sticky infected red cells (**cytoadherence**).

elim: Falciparum does not form hypnozoites; that is vivax and ovale.
Vivax prefers reticulocytes; falciparum infects red cells of all ages.
All human malaria is spread by Anopheles.
Antibodies do not cause the organ damage.

steps.x: **E. Infected red cells adhere to vascular endothelium.** Falciparum sequestration via cytoadherence explains cerebral malaria and AKI.
